ImageDescription.value: Bajra Shahi Mosque (Bengali: বজরা শাহী মসজিদ, romanized: Bojra Shahi Mosjid, Arabic: شاهي مسجد بجرا) is an 18th-century mosque located in the Bazra Union under Sonaimuri Upazila of Noakhali District.

Artist.value: Topu Saha

Categories.value: CC-Zero|Noakhali District|Bajra Shahi Mosque|Template Unknown (author)

ImageDescription.value:
Bajra Shahi Mosque (Bengali: বজরা শাহী মসজিদ) is a historically significant 18th-century mosque located at Bazra Union in Sonaimuri Upazila of Noakhali District, Bangladesh. The mosque was constructed in 1741–1742 CE during the reign of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah (1719–1748), a period marked by the regional consolidation of Mughal authority in eastern Bengal.

According to historical records, the mosque was commissioned by Amanullah, a local Mughal faujdar (military and administrative officer), as a congregational mosque for the surrounding settlements. It reflects the continuation of Mughal architectural traditions in Bengal even during the late Mughal period, when imperial power at the center was declining but provincial patronage of religious architecture remained active.

Architecturally, the mosque is built on an elevated rectangular plinth and follows the typical Mughal three-domed plan. The prayer hall is surmounted by three hemispherical domes resting on octagonal drums, with the central dome slightly larger than the flanking ones. The eastern façade features three arched entrances, the central arch being more prominent and richly ornamented. Slender octagonal minarets rise at the outer corners of the structure, capped with small domed kiosks, a characteristic feature of Mughal mosque architecture in Bengal.

One of the most distinctive aspects of the Bajra Shahi Mosque is its extensive surface decoration. The exterior walls and gateway are adorned with colorful ceramic tile mosaics and floral motifs, which are believed to have been added during later renovation phases, possibly in the 19th or early 20th century. These embellishments give the mosque a unique visual identity compared to earlier, more austere Mughal mosques in Bengal.

The mosque complex is enclosed by a boundary wall, with an ornate eastern entrance gateway leading to a spacious open courtyard. To the west of the mosque lies a large water reservoir (locally known as a dighi), which historically served the ritual ablution needs of worshippers and enhanced the environmental setting of the complex.

The Bajra Shahi Mosque is currently a protected monument under the Department of Archaeology of the Government of Bangladesh, recognizing its architectural, historical, and cultural significance. It continues to function as an active place of worship while also attracting researchers, historians, and visitors interested in Mughal-era Islamic architecture in southeastern Bengal.

This photograph shows the front (eastern) elevation of the mosque, highlighting its domes, decorative façade, minarets, and symmetrical layout within the landscaped surroundings.

ImageDescription.value:
Bajra Shahi Mosque is located in Bajra Union under Sonaimuri Upazila in Noakhali district. According to history, around 1741–42, Zamindar Amanullah excavated a large pond over 30 acres of land and built this attractive mosque beside it. The design of the mosque was inspired by the Jama Masjid in Delhi.

The mosque has three domes, which are made of marble stone. There is an arched entrance gate, and inside, the mihrab facing the qibla is decorated with intricate designs. It is widely believed that wishes made at Bajra Shahi Mosque are fulfilled. As a result, people from distant areas visit the mosque to make vows. How to get there

The distance from Maijdee town in Noakhali to Bajra Shahi Mosque is about 15 kilometers. You can reach the mosque by local bus heading toward Sonaimuri, or by CNG and auto-rickshaw.
